Weak Law of Large Numbers (text)
In the lesson 1, we discussed several approaches to define the probability of an event. One of them is the so-called frequentist approach, which suggests to estimate the unknown value of probability from the empirical data as the relative frequency of those experiments when the event \(A\) of interest occurs. By this approach, we consider the experiment in which the event \(A\) may happen and repeat it \(n\) times (with \(n\) large enough). Then record the number \(n_A\) of trials when \(A\) occurred and approximate the probability of \(A\) as \[P(A)\approx\frac{n_A}{n}.\] As we discussed there are several problems with this approach. First of all we do not know what \(n\) is large enough. Another problem is that even if we fix some \(n\) and two persons repeat the corresponding experiment independently \(n\) times they may get different values \(n_A\) and therefore we will get different values of the ratio \(\frac{n_A}{n}\). These problems are overcome if we take for the probability of \(A\) the limit of the considered ratio when \(n\) tends to infinity, i.e. \[P(A)=\lim_{n\rightarrow \infty}\frac{n_A}{n}.\] But it is still not clear whether this limit exists and if so is it indeed equal to the probability of \(A\). And the task of this section is to discus the law of large numbers which justifies this limit and explain in what sense it exists. Note that \[\frac{n_A}{n}=\frac{I_1+I_2+\dots+I_n}{n},\] where \(I_k\) is equal to \(1\) if \(A\) occurs in the \(k\)-th experiment and \(0\) if \(A\) does not occur, i.e., \(I_k\) is the indicator random variable of getting \(A\) in the \(k\)-th trial. Therefore the relative frequency of the event \(A\) is equal to the mean of the sequence of the indicator random variables of the event \(A\). More generally, let us consider an arbitrary sequence of independent identically distributed random variables \(X_1,X_2, \dots\) with \(\mathsf{E}(X_1) = \mu\) and \(\mathsf{Var}(X_1) = \sigma^2\). And set \[S_n = X_1 + \dots + X_n\] to be the sum of the first \(n\) of them. Then by independence, \[\mathsf{Var}(S_n) = n\sigma^2\] which implies that \(S_n\) spreads out with \(n\). Thus \(S_n\) cannot have a meaningful limit. For the sample mean\[ M_n := \frac{X_1+ \dots + X_n}n = \frac{S_n}n \] one finds that \[ \mathsf{E}(M_n) = \mu, \qquad \mathsf{Var}(M_n) = \frac{\sigma^2}n \] and thus \(M_n\) are concentrated near \(\mu\). Informally, the law of large numbers asserts that \(M_n\) converge to the true (theoretical) mean \(\mu\) as \(n\to\infty\). To derive it, apply Chebyshev's inequality to \(M_n\) and get \[ \mathsf{P}(|M_n - \mu| \ge {\varepsilon}) \le \frac{{\sigma^2}}{{n} {\varepsilon^2}} \] where the right hand side goes to zero as \(n\to\infty\). In fact, it is not necessary that \(X_k\) have finite \(\mathsf{Var}(X_k)\):
Theorem. Weak law of large numbers.
Let \(X_1, X_2, \dots\) be independent identically distributed random variables with mean \(\mu\). For every \(\varepsilon > 0\), we have, as \(n\to\infty\), \[ \boxed{ \mathsf{P}\bigl(|M_n - \mu| \ge \varepsilon\bigr) = \mathsf{P} \Bigl( \Bigl|\frac{X_1 + \dots + X_n}{n} - \mu\Bigr| \ge \varepsilon\Bigr) \to 0} \]
Example. If \(X_k\) have normal distribution \(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\), then by the weak law of large numbers, as \(n\to\infty\), \[\mathsf{P}\bigl(|M_n - \mu|\ge \varepsilon\bigr)\to 0.\] Indeed \(M_n \sim \mathcal{N}({\mu},{\sigma^2/n})\), and with \(Z:= {\sqrt{n}}(M_n - {\mu})/{\sigma} \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\) one finds \[ \mathsf{P}(|M_n - \mu| \ge \varepsilon) = \mathsf{P}(|Z| \ge \tfrac{\varepsilon \sqrt{n}}{\sigma}) = 2\mathsf{P}(Z \le - \tfrac{\varepsilon \sqrt{n}}{\sigma}) = 2 \Phi\Bigl(-\tfrac{\varepsilon \sqrt{n}}{\sigma}\Bigr) \to 0 \] as \(n\to\infty\).

Strong Law of Large Numbers (text)
In this section, we discuss the strong low of large numbers, which asserts the convergence of the sample means \(M_n\) of independent identically distributed random variables \(X_1\), \(X_2\), \(\dots\) to their mean in some other sense than the weak law of large numbers.
Definition (Convergence in probability)
A sequence of random variables \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) converges in probability to a random variable \(Y\) (written \(X_n \stackrel{\mathsf{P}}{\to} Y\)) if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), \[ \mathsf{P}\{|X_n - Y|\ge \varepsilon\} \to 0 \qquad \text{as} \qquad n\to\infty. \]
Thus the weak law of large numbers asserts that the sample means \(M_n\) of independent identically distributed random variables \(X_1\), \(X_2\), \(\dots\) with mean \(\mu\) converge to \(\mu\) in probability.
Definition (Converegence almost everywhere)
A sequence of random variables \(X_1, X_2,\dots\) converges almost everywhere (almost surely, with probability \(1\)) to a random variable \(X\) as \(n\to\infty\) (written \(X_n\stackrel{\mathrm{a.e.}}{\to} X\)) if \[\mathsf{P}\{\omega\in\Omega \mid X_n(\omega) \to X(\omega)\}=1\]
Example. Consider the sample space \(\Omega = [0,1]\) with the uniform probability measure. Then the random variables \(X_n(\omega) = \omega^n\) converge to \(0\) as \(n\to\infty\) if \(\omega\ne1\). Thus \(X_n\stackrel{\mathrm{a.e.}}{\to} 0\) as \(n\to\infty\).
Theorem
Convergence almost everywhere implies convergence in probability.
Example. (Convergent in probability but not almost everywhere.) Consider \(\Omega=[0,1]\) and set \(A_{k,n} = [k\cdot 2^{-n},(k+1)\cdot 2^{-n})\), \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), \(k=0,\dots, 2^n-1\) and \(X_{k,n} = \chi_{A_{k,n}}\). Then \(X_{k,n} \stackrel{\mathsf{P}}{\to} 0\) as \[\mathsf{P}\{|X_{k,n}|=1\}=\frac1{2^n},\] and so for any  \(\varepsilon >0\), as \(n\to\infty\)
\[\mathsf{P}\{|X_{k,n}-0|>\varepsilon\}\to 0.\] But \(X_{k,n}(\omega)\) diverge if \(\omega\ne1\)!
Theorem. Strong law of large numbers.
If \(X_1,X_2, \dots\) are independent identically distributed random variables with mean \(\mu\), then \(M_n = S_n/n \stackrel{\mathrm{a.e.}}{\to} \mu\).
Corollary. Estimating the c.d.f. Let \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) be i.i.d. random variables with c.d.f. \(F\). For \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), introduce the random variables \(I_k\) by \[ I_k(t;\omega) = \begin{cases} 0\qquad & \text{if}\quad X_k(\omega)>t\\ 1\qquad & \text{if}\quad X_k(\omega)\le t \end{cases} \] Then \(I_k(t)\) are independent and have Bernoulli distribution with parameter \(p:=F(t)\); thus \(\mathsf{E}(I_k(t)) = F(t)\) and by SLLN \[ \widehat{F}_{X,n}(t) := \frac{I_1(t)+ \dots + I_n(t)}n \to F(t) \] with probability \(1\).
Definition (Empirical c.d.f.)
Assume that \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) are i.i.d. random variables with c.d.f. \(F\) and \(x_k = X_k(\omega)\) is a realization of \(X_k\). The empirical c.d.f. \(\widehat{F}_{\mathbf{X},n}\) for realization \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1,\dots,x_n)\) is given by \[ \widehat{F}_{\mathbf{x},n}(t) := \frac{\sharp\{k \mid x_k \le t\}}n \]
Clearly, \(\widehat{F}_{\mathbf{x},n}(t) = \widehat{F}_{\mathbf{X},n}(t;\omega)\) is a realization of the random variable \(\widehat{F}_{\mathbf{X},n}(t)\);
therefore, \(\forall t\), \(\widehat{F}_{\mathbf{x},n}(t)\to F(t)\) with probability \(1\), i.e., the empirical c.d.f. almost surely converges to theoretical c.d.f. as \(n\to\infty\)
The convergence is even stronger in view of the following
Theorem (Glivenko–Cantelli)
Almost surely, as \(n\to\infty\),  \[ \sup _{t\in \mathbb {R} }|\widehat{F}_{\mathbf{X},n}(t)-F(t)| \longrightarrow 0 \] i.e., with probability \(1\) the empirical cumulative distribution function \(\widehat{F}_{\mathbf{X},n}\) converges to \(F\) uniformly.

Central Limit Theorem (text)
In this section, we discuss the central limit theorem, which is one of the most remarkable results in probability theory. Loosely speaking, it states that the sum of a large number of independent random variables has a distribution that is approximately normal. Hence, it provides a simple method for computing approximate probabilities for sums of independent random variables. Also, it implies that probabilistic and statistical methods that work for normal distributions can be applicable to many problems involving other types of distributions. To derive the central limit theorem, we need to consider the notion of characteristic functions.
Definition (Characteristic function)
The characteristic function of a random variable \(X\) is \[\boxed{\phi_X(t):= \mathsf{E}(e^{itX})}.\] Thus the characteristic function is the Fourier transform of the p.d.f. of the random variable \(X\).
Remark.  Observe that characteristic function is related to the moment generating function of \(X\) via the equality \[\phi_X(t)=M_X(it).\] Recall that the moment generating function need not be defined for \(s\ne0\). For example, for the Cauchy distribution with \(f(x) = \pi^{-1}(1+x^2)^{-1}\) m.g.f. in not defined. On the contrary, the characteristic function is well defined for all \(t\in\mathbb{R}\).
Properties of characteristic functions.
Uniqueness: \(\phi_X\) determines uniquely the distribution of \(X\);
Derivatives of characteristic functions are related to moments: \(\phi_X^{(k)}(0) = i^k\mu_k(X)\);
For independent \(X\) and \(Y\), \(\phi_{X+Y} = \phi_X \cdot \phi_Y\).
Example (Normal distribution). Let \(X\) be a random variable with normal distribution \(\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\). Then its characteristic function \begin{align*} {\phi_X(t)} &= \mathsf{E}(e^{itX}) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \exp\Bigl\{\frac{2i\sigma^2tx-(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr\}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}\\ &= \int_{\mathbb{R}} \exp\Bigl\{-\frac{(x-\mu-it\sigma^2)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr\} \frac{dx}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma} \exp\Bigl\{i\mu t-\sigma^2 t^2/2\Bigr\}\\ &= \exp\Bigl\{i\mu t-\sigma^2 t^2/2\Bigr\} \end{align*}  as \({\int_{\mathbb{R}} \exp\Bigl\{-\frac{(x-\mu-it\sigma^2)^2}{2\sigma^2}\Bigr\} \frac{dx}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma} = 1}\). The calculations might be simplified by considering a standard normal r.v. \(Z\) such that \(X = \mu + \sigma Z\) and observing that \[\phi_X(t) = e^{i\mu t} \phi_Z(\sigma t).\]Thus for independent random variables \(X_k \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_k,\sigma^2_k)\) \[\phi_{X_1+X_2+\cdots+X_n}(t)=\exp\Bigl\{i\sum \mu_k t-\sum\sigma^2_k t^2/2\Bigr\},\] which by uniqueness of characteristic function implies that the distribution of the sum of these random variables is normal: \[X_1 + \dots + X_n \sim\mathcal{N}(\sum \mu_k, \sum \sigma^2_k).\]
Example (Exponential distribution).For exponential random variable \(X \sim \mathcal{E}(\lambda)\), \[ \phi_X(t) = \mathsf{E}(e^{itX}) = \int_0^\infty \lambda e^{-(\lambda-it) x} dx = \frac{\lambda}{\lambda - it}. \] If \(X_1,X_2 \sim \mathcal{E}(\lambda)\) are independent, then \(X_1 + X_2\) is not(!) exponentially distributed as \[\phi_{X_1 + X_2} = \phi_{X_1}\cdot \phi_{X_2}\] is not(!) a characteristic function of \(\mathcal{E}(\mu)\).
In the central limit theorem, we encounter another type of convergence, namely convergence in law.
Definition (Converge in law)
Random variables \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) converge in law to a random variable \(X\) if \[ F_{X_n}(t) \to F_X(t) \qquad \text{as} \quad n\to\infty \] for all points of continuity of \(F_X\).
Example (Poisson approximation). Poisson theorem states that the binomial random variables \(X_n\sim\mathcal{B}(n,p_n)\) converge in law to the Poisson distribution \(\mathcal{P}(\lambda)\) if \(np_n \to \lambda\) as \(n\to\infty\).
Theorem.
Convergence in law is equivalent to the convergence of characteristic functions.
Assume \(X_1,X_2,\dots\) are independent random variables with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\). Recall that the total sum \(S_n:=X_1+\dots + X_n\) has mean \(n\mu\) and variance \(n\sigma^2\) blowing up as \(n\) increases and thus \(S_n\) cannot converge, in any sense. On the other hand, the sample means \(M_n:=S_n/n\) converge to the constant value \(\mu\) by the strong law of large numbers and \(\mathsf{Var}(M_n)=\sigma^2/n\to0\). And what in the intermediate case; can we get a non-trivial limit under a different scaling of \(S_n\)?
Let us consider the standardized sums \[ Z_n : = \frac{\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}(M_n-\mu) = \frac{S_n - \mu n}{\sigma \sqrt{n}}. \] The central limit theorem asserts that \(Z_n\) converge in law to the standard Gaussian random variable \(Z\sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\).
Theorem. Central Limit Theorem.
Under the above assumptions, \(Z_n\) converge in law to \(Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)\), i.e., for every \(t\in\mathbb{R}\) \[ \mathsf{P}\Bigl\{\frac{X_1 + \dots + X_n- n\mu}{\sigma\sqrt{n}}\le t\Bigr\} \to \Phi(t) \] Moreover, the convergence is uniform on \(\mathbb{R}\).
Sketch of the proof. To prove the statement of the theorem, it is enough to establish convergence of the characteristic functions of \(Z_n\) to that of \(Z\). Set \(Y_k = (X_k - \mu)/\sigma\); then \(Z_n = (Y_1+\dots + Y_n)/\sqrt{n}\) and \[\phi_{Z_n}(t) = \Bigl[\phi_{Y_1}\bigl(\tfrac{t}{\sqrt{n}}\bigr)\Bigr]^n. \] Now \(\phi_{Y_1}\bigl(\tfrac{t}{\sqrt{n}}\bigr) = 1 - t^2/2n + o(n^{-1})\). Recall that \((1 + x/n)^n \to e^x\); therefore, \[ \phi_{Z_n} (t) \approx (1- t^2/2n)^n \to e^{-t^2/2} = \phi_Z(t). \]
Example (Post office overweight). Assume that a post office gets every day appr. 100 parcels whose weight is uniformly distributed in the interval \(1\) to \(10\) kg. What is the probability that the total weight will not be greater than \(500\) kg?
Solution:
Denote by \(X_n\) the weight of the \(n^{\mathrm{th}}\) parcel and set \[S_{100}:=X_1 + \dots+X_{100}\]
As \(\mathsf{E}(X_k)=11/2\) and \(\mathsf{Var}(X_k)= 27/4\), we conclude that \begin{align*} \mathsf{P}(S_{100}\le 500) &= \mathsf{P}(S_{100}-550\le -50) \\ &= \mathsf{P}\Bigl(\frac{S_{100} - 550}{10\sqrt{27/4}} \le -\frac{10}{3\sqrt3}\Bigr) \approx \Phi(-1.925) = 0.027 \end{align*}
Note that (one-sided) Chebyshev's inequality gives \[ \mathsf{P}(S_{100} \le 500) = \mathsf{P}(S_{100}-550\le -50) \le \frac{27\cdot 25} {27\cdot 25 + 50^2} \le 0.213. \]
